output:
I let the silence stretch a moment longer than Perrin expects from me. The kid's nervous about the debt we all know about but don't speak of—but this morning it's just breakfast. Let them carry one thing at a time.

"Now then," I say, finally. "Check the pot by the stove. There's barley from yesterday, still good. Enough for you and Liora both if she'll have it cold."

I don't mention that I ate my share already, walking the numbers in my head last night. Four hundred to Marta. I've got four hundred set aside in the ledger, have had it for weeks. Haven't told Bram. Won't tell him. He'd rather dig for copper that isn't there than take his wife's charity.

But the kid needs to eat, and Liora's household has enough weight on it too.

I look at Tobias, who's already moving toward the door, then at Nell with her hands in her clay. "I'm to market," I say, though they know my days well as I do. "Harvey Oak first, then we'll see what's walking."

I need to move. Need to see what's surplus in this town before the morning's half gone, and whether I can turn a few sim into enough to carry us through. The debt to Marta can wait another day. It always waits.

I pick up my coat.

I stand in the silence after Nell's footsteps fade. Perrin's still here, waiting on an answer I already gave once and they didn't hear. Tobias too, though he's halfway out the door already, questions tumbling over each other like pebbles.

"Now then," I say, and let the quiet settle before I continue. Cold barley in the pot by the stove. Enough for two if Liora's willing." I meet Perrin's eye. "You know Marta would give you bread on credit. She has before. But that debt compounds, and you're not the one paying it yet."

I turn to Tobias, who's still hovering. "Marta's bread costs twelve sim a loaf now. We owe her enough already." I don't say Bram's name. Don't need to. "The barley's free, and it's paid for. That's what we have."

Perrin's smart enough to understand what I'm not saying—take what's ours, don't borrow more weight. But I also know a kid walking to college with their pride and an empty stomach. Liora's at least as hungry, and the Thornes aren't short but they ain't wasteful either.

"I'll be at Harvey Oak by seven," I say, moving toward the door myself now. "If there's flour cheap, I'll bring it home. If there's not, we eat what we have."

I pause at the threshold, looking back at both of them—my brother by blood, my child by choice, both of them carrying Holloway stubbornness like a birthright.

"Eat the barley," I say. "Both of you. I'll find more before noon."

Then I walk out, because staying means answering more questions I don't have answers to, and the market waits for no one.

I let myself look at Bram long enough to see what's under the words. The copper thinning—five weeks he's carried that alone. And the debt paid, which means he found 400 sim from somewhere, or earned it, or borrowed from someone else to close what he owed Marta. Pride will hollow a man out worse than hunger.

"Now then," I say, and the silence stretches. "The seam running thin. Iron's harder work, you said. You have numbers on what that costs us?"

But he's asked about food, and Perrin's asked, and Tobias, and I haven't answered any of them yet. Too busy walking in my head to walk in the world.

"There's barley in the pot," I say, finally. "Cold, but edible. Enough for two if Perrin brings Liora." I pause. "Marta's bread costs twelve now. We don't owe her, you paid that—but we don't have bread either. I was walking to market to see."

The words come slower now because I'm choosing them. I've got 400 sim put aside, marked for Marta, and Bram telling me the debt's cleared. Which means I have 400 sim I didn't have yesterday, and a household that's hungry now.

"Tell me where you found 400 sim," I say. "Then tell me what you need from me."

But first I need to move, or the morning'll be gone and I'll have let another Holloway family trade their silence for my inaction.
